paper_title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents that reason, use tools, and interact with executable environments to solve increasingly complex tasks. An agents capabilities arise from both its underlying model and its harness: the prompts, tools, middleware, and control logic that mediate its interaction with the environment. Even with model weights fixed, modifying these components can substantially improve agent performance (LangChain, 2026). This has motivated growing interest in automatic harness optimization (AHO) (Lee et al., 2026; Park et al., 2026), in which an external optimizer diagnoses execution traces and updates the surrounding harness to improve the task agent. Most existing AHO methods optimize primarily for task quality, whereas real-world deployment must also consider execution cost and other requirements such as safety and privacy. Here, we focus on jointly optimizing task response quality and LLM token cost. Deployment preferences may specify fixed qualitycost trade-off, impose an explicit constraint, or defer selection among Pareto Work done during an internship at Microsoft. This multi-objective setting raises key question beyond final deployment selection: which intermediate harness updates should remain available for continued optimization? This distinction is particularly important for AHO methods with staged evaluation, where locally generated updates are screened before receiving broader development evaluation (Park et al., 2026). The screening decision does more than reduce evaluation cost: it also determines which intermediate harnesses remain available for subsequent refinement. Applying the final deployment preference directly at this stage can therefore prematurely reject updates whose immediate qualitycost trade-off is unfavorable but whose changes enable stronger solutions later, consistent with prior optimization research showing that search guidance need not coincide with the ultimate objective (Knowles et al., 2001; Lehman & Stanley, 2011). For long-horizon agents, this mismatch can arise naturally because execution cost is often coupled with task progress: harness may appear inexpensive simply because some executions terminate prematurely, whereas patch that fixes such failures may improve quality while increasing cost through additional reasoning or environment interaction. Rejecting the update solely because it temporarily violates the deployment cost preference can prevent later patches from building on its capability gains and reducing the newly exposed inefficiencies. Local promotion is further complicated by stochastic execution. Repeated runs of the same harness can vary substantially in both quality and cost, so an apparent improvement may reflect execution randomness rather than the update itself. Simply comparing mean outcomes collapses this variation into point estimate and can therefore overstate weakly supported gains. Staged multi-objective AHO thus faces two questions: what intermediate movements are worth preserving for further optimization, and how can we assess whether their observed gains are statistically supported? To address these issues, we introduce ParetoSaddler, framework for staged qualitycost harness optimization that separates exploration-time promotion from deployment-time selection. At each iteration, an underlying AHO method constructs candidate harness from execution evidence. ParetoSaddler repeatedly evaluates the candidate and its parent and uses Bayesian bootstrap support (Rubin, 1981) to promote updates showing credible progress in either quality or cost, without requiring them to already satisfy the final deployment preference. Only after the optimization budget is exhausted is that preference applied to select the final harness. In this way, ParetoSaddler separates what is worth exploring during optimization from what is ultimately worth deploying. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark (Meng et al., 2026) and GAIA2 (Froger et al., 2026) using domain-disjoint training, development, and test splits under both Pareto-set optimization and Preprint quality-constrained cost minimization. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality on the heldout test set from 70.86% to 81.35% while reducing cost from $1.17 to $1.01 per task; on GAIA2, quality improves from 56.22% to 62.89% while cost decreases from $0.78 to $0.45. Notably, its quality-oriented Pareto solution also outperforms quality-only harness optimization by 7.49 points on ClawMark and 5.56 points on GAIA2 while remaining cheaper, showing that jointly optimizing quality and cost need not sacrifice quality and can even lead the search to stronger quality solutions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: When performing multi-objective agent harness optimization with staged evaluation, we identify mismatch between intermediate promotion and final deployment selection, where enforcing deployment preferences too early can prune updates useful for later optimization. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which combines Pareto-aware promotion, repeated execution, and Bayesian bootstrap screening for effective and reliable qualitycost harness optimization. We demonstrate consistent qualitycost improvements on ClawMark and GAIA2, supported by detailed analyses and ablations of promotion, repeated execution, and Bayesian screening.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Automatic Harness Optimization. Automatic optimization of LLM systems has expanded from prompts (Pryzant et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2026) and reusable skills (Yang et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026) to complete agent harnesses. Existing AHO methods broadly follow two optimization protocols. Search-based approaches (Lou et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026) generate and compare harness candidates using execution feedback, iteratively refining promising candidates. Learning-based approaches (Park et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026) derive incremental updates from mini-batches and use staged evaluation to decide which updates to retain. These protocols are orthogonal to whether adaptation occurs online during deployment or offline on fixed development corpus. ParetoSaddler follows the staged offline-learning setting and focuses on joint qualitycost optimization. Multi-Objective Optimization for LLM Systems. Classical multi-objective optimization retains non-dominated solutions representing different trade-offs (Knowles & Corne, 2000; Zitzler et al., 2001), and recent work applies this principle to prompts (Yang & Li, 2023; Sinha et al., 2024; Bussing et al., 2026) and agent skills (Gong et al., 2026). Full-harness optimization is more costly because evaluating each candidate requires long agent trajectories, motivating staged evaluation that reserves broader evaluation for promising candidates (Schmucker et al., 2021). Prior work shows that search guidance need not coincide with the final selection objective (Knowles et al., 2001; Lehman & Stanley, 2011). Building on this distinction, ParetoSaddler uses Pareto-aware promotion during optimization while reserving the deployment preference for final harness selection. Optimization under Stochastic Evaluation. Candidate selection under noisy evaluations is longstanding challenge in optimization (Branke & Schmidt, 2003; Marceau-Caron & Schoenauer, 2014). Recent work has applied repeated evaluation and bootstrap resampling to multi-objective ranking and LLM-agent configuration selection (Rook et al., 2024; Vattikonda et al., 2025). ParetoSaddler builds on this by incorporating Bayesian bootstrap uncertainty estimation (Rubin, 1981) into staged AHO, using statistical support to determine candidate promotion.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Benchmarks, Agents, and Data Splits. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on two challenging longhorizon agent benchmarks: ClawMark (Meng et al., 2026) and GAIA2 (Froger et al., 2026). For both benchmarks, we construct domain-disjoint training, development, and test splits, such that harness updates are evaluated on previously unseen domains. For ClawMark, we use 92 tasks with stage-0 rubrics and optimize OpenClaw (OpenClaw, 2026) with GPT-5.4 at high reasoning effort. For GAIA2, we follow the same split configuration as AutoSaddler (Park et al., 2026) and optimize the benchmarks default ReAct-style harness using GPT-5.5 with medium reasoning effort. Instantiation and Baselines. We instantiate ParetoSaddler on top of AutoSaddler. For deployment preferences, we study two representative settings: (i) Pareto-set optimization, where no specific qualitycost preference is specified in advance, and (ii) quality-constrained cost minimization, where cost is minimized subject to required quality level. We compare ParetoSaddler against two baselines. (i) Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) is representative harness-optimization method without staged evaluation, iteratively updating the harness using the full training set. We adapt MH to the two deployment preferences considered above. (ii) AutoSaddler (Park et al., 2026) serves as our single-objective, quality-oriented baseline, allowing us to assess whether jointly optimizing quality and cost comes at the expense of quality improvement. For conciseness, we denote the evaluated methodpreference combinations as PS-PARETO and PS-MINCOST for ParetoSaddler under Pareto-set optimization and quality-constrained cost minimization, respectively; MH-PARETO and MH-MINCOST for the corresponding Meta-Harness variants; and AS-QUALITY for our quality-only AutoSaddler adaptation. For Pareto-set optimization, we select two representative harnesses from the development Pareto set for test evaluation: the quality-extreme harness (e.g., PS-PARETOQ) and the cost-extreme harness (e.g., PS-PARETOC). Experimental Protocol. We use the GitHub Copilot SDK (GitHub, 2026) with GPT-5.5 at xhigh reasoning effort as the optimizer for all methods (usage reported in Appendix G). Unless otherwise stated, each task is evaluated with = 3 rollouts, and ParetoSaddler and AutoSaddler use training mini-batches of three tasks. For Bayesian screening, we use = 10,000 bootstrap draws, prespecified promotion threshold of γ = 0.7, and local quality-loss allowance of ϵQ = 0.1. We impose no upper bound on local cost increases, setting ϵC = +. Moreover, for PS-MINCOST we require the quality to remain within 10 percentage points below that of the initial harness. We measure response quality using normalized stage-0 rubric score on ClawMark, and Pass@1 on GAIA2, and report token-based execution cost in USD per task. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix A. 5.2 MAIN RESULTS Table 1 reports the performance of development-selected harnesses on the domain-disjoint test sets, while Figure 1 shows their evolution in qualitycost space on the development set. ParetoSaddler improves both quality and cost on unseen domains. The quality-extreme PSPARETOQ achieves the highest mean test quality on both benchmarks while reducing cost relative to the initial harness. On ClawMark, it improves quality by 14.8% (70.86% to 81.35%) while reducing cost by 13.7% ($1.17 to $1.01); on GAIA2, it improves quality by 11.9% (56.22% to 62.89%) while reducing cost by 42.3% ($0.78 to $0.45 per task). The cost-extreme PS-PARETOC also improves quality and reduces cost on both benchmarks. Both operating points outperform their corresponding Meta-Harness variants in mean quality and cost on both benchmarks. These gains are consistent across all three held-out GAIA2 universes (see Appendix for additional stability analysis). Joint optimization does not sacrifice quality, and may even improve it. Despite optimizing both quality and cost, PS-PARETOQ outperforms the quality-only AS-QUALITY baseline by 7.49 quality points on ClawMark and 5.56 points on GAIA2, while also reducing cost on both benchmarks. This is somewhat unexpected result: introducing the cost objective is associated with better, rather than merely preserved, quality. This enables distinct qualityand cost-oriented harnesses to be selected after optimization according to the deployment preference. 5.3 ANALYSIS AND ABLATION STUDIES RQ1: How does Pareto-aware promotion enable better optimization outcomes? We examine the promotion decisions on ClawMark, with complementary GAIA2 cases in Appendix C. Pareto-set vs. quality-only optimization. I-7 in PSPARETO provides representative example (Figure 7). Its parent achieves perfect quality on all three minibatch tasks across three executions. I-7 reduces mean mini-batch cost by 17.22% with 1.33-point quality decrease, which the quality gate would reject. Paretoaware promotion instead advances I-7 to development evaluation, where it improves both quality (72.94% vs. 72.27%) and cost ($0.88 vs. $1.13). Its boundedprobing and completion-control behaviors persist in later iterations, contributing to the selected harness. Figure 3: ClawMark optimization trajectories and final test results of PS-MINCOST under Pareto and MinCost local gates. Faint markers denote evaluated candidates not selected for subsequent refinement. Controlled gate ablation. Because the preceding analysis is observational, we next perform controlled study by replacing Pareto-aware promotion with deployment-oriented MinCost Local Gate in the PS-MINCOST setting. Figure 3 shows that this change produces markedly different search trajectories. The Pareto gate promotes 11 candidates, compared with only three under the MinCost Local Gate, and reaches better test operating 8 Preprint point. The key divergence occurs around I-11, before which the Pareto trajectory approaches similar cost wall to the MinCost Local Gate, near the dashed line in Figure 3. I-11 improves mini-batch quality from 83.65% to 87.62% while increasing cost by 10.5%. The MinCost gate would reject this update, whereas Pareto promotion retains it for development evaluation and subsequent refinement toward I-14 and I-16. Without admitting this intermediate update, the Pareto trajectory would likely remain trapped near the same local cost minima as the MinCost Local Gate. Together, these results show that Pareto-aware promotion enables better optimization by preserving intermediate states whose local trade-offs may appear suboptimal, but whose value emerges through broader evaluation and subsequent refinement. RQ2: How do repeated executions improve harness optimization? We ask what additional evidence repeated executions provide and whether this evidence improves optimization outcomes. Diagnostic value of repeated executions. Repeated runs reveal three types of evidence that single trajectory cannot provide: (i) persistent failures, where repeated failure across runs indicates recurring defects; (ii) mixed outcomes, where quality variation on the same task provides direct contrast for unstable behaviors; and (iii) efficiency contrast, where all runs succeed but differ substantially in execution cost. Table 7 provides more details. Repeated executions also strengthen patch verification and promotion: preand post-patch comparisons reveal whether an improvement persists, while repeated observations provide more reliable evidence for promotion than single atypical execution. Single-run vs. three-run optimization. As the analysis above is again observational, we perform controlled endto-end ablation within the PS-PARETO setting, varying only the number of executions per task from one to three while keeping the remaining optimization setup fixed. Table 2 shows that three-run optimization reaches stronger held-out operating points. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced ParetoSaddler, framework for staged qualitycost harness optimization that separates intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. On ClawMark and GAIA2, its Pareto-selected harnesses achieve higher quality at lower execution cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analyses and ablations show that Pareto-aware promotion preserves intermediate candidates that can enable later improvements, repeated executions provide richer and more reliable evidence for optimization, and Bayesian screening filters candidates whose apparent qualitycost gains are weakly supported under execution uncertainty. These findings highlight the value of preserving intermediate trade-offs and accounting for execution uncertainty in harness optimization.

sections.content: We used generative AI tools to assist with writing and polishing manuscript sections. We have not used generative AI tools for research ideation, methodology, or experimental design. All research concepts and analyses were developed and conducted by the authors. The authors reviewed the AIassisted text, checked numerical claims against experimental records, and verified cited sources. We take full responsibility for the final manuscript, including its claims, results, and conclusions.

sections.title: 8 PRIVACY AND RESPONSIBLE AI CONSIDERATIONS
sections.content: Privacy. Our experiments use publicly available benchmarks, ClawMark and GAIA2, and do not involve the collection of new real-user data. We do not investigate privacy-preserving mechanisms or evaluate the privacy implications of deploying optimized agent harnesses in real-world applications. Scope and Responsible AI. This work focuses on optimizing agent task quality and execution cost in benchmark environments. We do not evaluate fairness, harmlessness, safety, or broader societal impacts. Consequently, improvements in quality and cost should not be interpreted as evidence of safety or readiness for unrestricted real-world deployment.

sections.title: 9 REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We have made every effort to support the reproducibility of the results presented in this paper. Section 4 and Appendix describe the method and provide pseudocode for the general framework and its AutoSaddler instantiation. Section 5.1 and Appendix document the benchmark splits, model configurations, adaptations, optimization schedules, and other experimental setup details. Appendix presents annotated optimization trajectories, while Appendices and document complete runs. Appendix provides selected optimizer prompt excerpts. Both benchmarks, ClawMark and GAIA2, are publicly available.

sections.title: A ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: Benchmarks and Data Splits. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on two long-horizon agent benchmarks with complementary execution settings. ClawMark (Meng et al., 2026) evaluates multi-turn, multiday coworker agents across stateful professional scenarios, covering realistic workflows that involve persistent state, tool use, and rule-based evaluation. GAIA2 (Froger et al., 2026) evaluates agents in dynamic and asynchronous environments, where the environment may evolve independently of agent actions and tasks require sustained interaction with external services. We construct training, development, and test splits at the group level rather than randomly partitioning individual tasks. This prevents closely related tasks from the same group from appearing in both optimization and evaluation, and tests whether harness updates learned during optimization transfer to previously unseen task groups. The same splits are fixed before optimization and shared by all methods. For ClawMark, we restrict evaluation to initial-stage tasks with explicit stage-0 rubrics to keep repeated evaluations across optimization candidates within the available execution budget. Later-stage adaptation is outside the scope of this evaluation. For GAIA2, we follow the split protocol of AutoSaddler (Park et al., 2026). The resulting assignments are summarized in Table 4. Table 4: Group-disjoint benchmark splits. ClawMark is partitioned by scenario and GAIA2 by Universe. Numbers in parentheses denote the number of tasks. Subsequent calls use the reported fresh-input and cache-read token counts at their respective rates. This convention prevents pre-existing cache state from discounting the initial call in the reported execution cost. Deployment Settings. We evaluate two settings for deployment preference: Pareto-set optimization and quality-constrained cost minimization. The symmetric setting of cost-constrained quality maximization can be handled analogously. We do not separately evaluate weighted-sum scalarization, as its fixed scalar objective can be optimized by existing single-objective AHO methods. Benchmark Adaptation. All ClawMark experiments use OpenClaw v2026.6.9. We adapt ClawMark to reduce cross-run interference during parallel evaluation. Each execution receives unique Notion root, replacing shared evaluation-hub cleanup with execution-scoped teardown. For Google Sheets, we retain per-execution Drive folders and strengthen exact-ID resource lookup. Executionspecific resource IDs are injected into each stages agent context and reused in checker-side resolution, while tool-use guidance discourages global title-based discovery. These changes preserve task objectives and rubric criteria. Preprint Baseline Adaptation. We adapt AutoSaddler and Meta-Harness to the same benchmark environments and monetary-cost accounting used by ParetoSaddler, while preserving their distinct search and selection mechanisms. Because the methods differ in their evaluation structure, we report their evaluation schedules and repetition counts explicitly rather than forcing an identical protocol. For AutoSaddler (Park et al., 2026), we use its quality-only configuration, denoted AS-QUALITY. We combine its separate capabilityand steering-oriented optimization phases into unified search loop, allowing the optimizer to apply either or both types of changes within each iteration. This aligns the available edit choices with ParetoSaddler and avoids confounding the comparison of optimization objectives with fixed phase schedule. Each task is executed three times, with quality averaged across executions before aggregation across tasks. We also apply comparable Bayesianbootstrap test when deciding whether to promote local candidate based on quality alone, using the same promotion threshold γ. Proposal generation and candidate selection therefore remain qualityoriented; execution cost is only recorded for evaluation but is not used as an optimization objective or promotion criterion. For Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), we retain its history-conditioned proposal and evaluation loop without introducing staged evaluation. We instantiate two objective-specific variants. MH-PARETO receives both quality and monetary-cost feedback, maintains the nondominated qualitycost frontier, and draws proposal parents from this frontier. MH-MINCOST instead minimizes mean execution cost subject to the baseline-relative quality constraint Q(h) max{0, Q(h0) ϵ}, using the same absolute tolerance ϵ as PS-MINCOST. The lowest-cost feasible candidate serves as the selection reference, while other historical candidates still contribute to subsequent proposals. Optimization Details. Unless otherwise stated, we use = 3 executions per task. This choice reflects the substantial cost of repeatedly executing long-horizon agents across optimization candidates and the available evaluation budget. With only three executions, rare outcomes may remain unobserved, and estimates of execution variability and bootstrap promotion support may be sensitive to the observed runs, particularly for candidates near the promotion threshold. Larger repetition counts could improve statistical precision but would require additional evaluation resources. We use = 10,000 independent Bayesian bootstrap draws, limiting the Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated promotion support to at most 0.005. These draws reuse the recorded observations and require no additional LLM calls. The cost safeguard is disabled by setting ϵC = +. This is because substantial local cost increase can still reflect genuine task progress. For example, resolving premature termination may result in substantial task progress while requiring more reasoning or environment interactions, making the cost increase difficult to estimate beforehand. ParetoSaddler and AS-QUALITY perform one optimization epoch over the training split using minibatches of three tasks. This yields 17 proposal iterations on ClawMark and 25 on GAIA2. Unless otherwise stated, each task is executed three times. The task model and its inference configuration remain fixed throughout optimization. Meta-Harness uses its original full-set evaluation structure rather than staged evaluation. Each proposed harness is evaluated on the combined training and development search set. We run MetaHarness for 8 proposal iterations on ClawMark and 15 on GAIA2, giving Meta-Harness approximately 1.37 and 1.22 the maximum task-execution budgets of the staged methods on ClawMark and GAIA2, respectively. We allocate Meta-Harness larger evaluation budget to avoid favoring the methods using staged evaluation through additional optimization compute.

We complement the ClawMark analysis in Section 5.3 with case studies from the GAIA2 PS-PARETO run. We focus on I-9 and I-17, whose mini-batches achieve perfect quality. Iteration I-9 achieves perfect quality on all three mini-batch tasks across all three executions before applying patches. Nevertheless, the execution traces expose unnecessary retrieval overhead: successful aggregation workflows retain full email bodies and perform individual contact lookups. I-9 then introduces compact, date-filtered email reads and batched contact lookup, reducing the amount of information retrieved and the number of separate lookup operations required. After the update, screening quality remains at 100%, while mean cost decreases from $0.824 to $0.494 per task, by 40.02%. Since every observed quality score is 100% for both harnesses, the quality-only gate would reject the promotion because it requires strict quality improvement. The Pareto gate instead assigns promotion support of 1.0 and advances I-9 to development evaluation. On the development set, I-9 improves both objectives relative to its parent: quality increases from 54.36% to 55.90%, while cost decreases from $0.64 to $0.54 per task, leading to better development operating point. I-17 provides another example involving both evidence access and execution control. sections.title: K OPTIMIZER PROMPTS
sections.content: Building on AutoSaddlers multi-session optimizer, ParetoSaddler extends the session instructions to account for both response quality and execution cost. We present selected additions and replacements, relative to the corresponding quality-only templates. The boxes reproduce selected passages with line wrapping adjusted; [...] marks omissions, and braces denote runtime placeholders. Promotion and archive decisions are computed by the outer optimization loop, rather than by the optimizers textual assessment. Candidate Preparation (Session 0). The evolution session uses development-set qualitycost measurements and archive membership to prepare the next candidate. In the template shown here, the outer loop fixes the current parent; the optimizer may repair uncompensated regressions or transfer localized mechanisms from eligible archive members. Session 0: Candidate Preparation Modified Instructions ## Goal Prepare the already-forked current harness source tree for this iteration's multi-objective optimization patch. The objective is to grow the Pareto frontier by maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost. The outer loop has already selected the `CURRENT` base; Session 0 must not reselect or replace it. Preparation must be **data-driven**, based on full-development objective vectors, MOO status, outcome analysis, execution traces, and focused source comparison - not attachment to accumulated patches or single-objective ranking. [...] 32 Preprint ## Candidate Performance {candidate_table} [...] ## Preparation Strategy The current child is always the starting point. Choose among these actions: - **Keep the current fork unchanged** when no evidence-backed Pareto-relevant preparation is warranted. - **Repair an inherited Pareto regression** by reverting only lines that caused quality loss or cost growth without compensating objective gain. - **Transfer Pareto mechanism** when donor has measured, localized quality, cost, or joint improvement that complements the current child. [...] The resulting source must remain descendant of the fixed current fork. Donor use adds provenance; it does not change the base parent. DiagnosisPatch (Session 1). Diagnosis is extended from unsuccessful tasks to cost-inefficient executions, including tasks that already pass. The session receives measured cost and per-run evidence alongside quality scores, and is instructed to inspect repeated executions before making causal or variance claims. The objective permits quality improvements, cost improvements, and trade-offs, while explicitly guarding against savings obtained by omitting required work. Session 1: DiagnosisPatch Modified Instructions ## Goal Fix incomplete or cost-inefficient scenarios in this mini-batch by diagnosing root causes from execution traces and the agent codebase, then applying targeted code patches without regressing scenarios that already pass. [...] The optimization objective is to grow useful **quality-cost Pareto frontier** across the full task distribution, not just this mini-batch. Joint improvements, quality-improving, or cost-improving are all valid. Patches should address general behavioral patterns, not hardcode scenario-specific answers. [...] Do not create cheap failure by removing required work or validation. [...] ## Initial Measured Cost {cost_listing} ### Cost breakdown - every task Preprint Token and artifact breakdown for **each** task below. When repeated runs are enabled, each task also lists per-run score, cost, token counters, and trace paths. {cost_breakdown} [...] ### 2. Diagnose failing or expensive scenarios For each failing scenario or expensive run, use the `diagnose` skill to identify the root cause. The key is to find **why** the agent made the wrong decision or became costly, not just **what** went wrong. Diagnosis requires reading both the execution trace and the agent codebase. Use the exact per-run artifact paths in the cost breakdown to inspect harness output. Start with `run/output.jsonl` for score, status, rationale, and exception state; then read the matching lite trace for agent behavior and input/cache/output token usage. Escalate to the matching full trace for environment, app-state, event, or judge evidence. For `num_runs > 1`, inspect every retained run before making causal or variance claims; for `num_runs = 1`, the single row and trace are the complete run-level evidence. Use only these benchmark artifacts for execution and cost attribution. Reflection (Session 2). Reflection separately records measured objective movement, evidence that the intended mechanism was exercised, and attribution to the patch or execution variability. It asks whether additional work supports quality and whether cost reductions preserve required behavior. ## Objective history (accuracy up, cost down) Session 2: Reflection Modified Instructions Per-candidate measured cost/task and accuracy so far. The archive contains every nondominated vector; it is not ranked into one champion. {objective_history} ### Full-validation interpretation {full_validation_context} When C{candidate_idx} has measured full-validation row: 1. Compare its cost and accuracy with the seed, immediate parent, current, and other Pareto archive members. 2. Check whether the same-minibatch cost direction held at full-validation scale. 3. Attribute the aggregate movement only to mechanisms supported by the patch and available evidence; do not invent per-scenario validation behavior. 4. Record the conclusion through `--generalization-note` on the relevant scenario reflections. If C{candidate_idx} has no measured row, say that generalization is unmeasured rather than inferring it from prior candidates. [...] Never rewrite these machine-computed decisions from trace interpretation. 34 Preprint Separately classify whether the intended mechanism was exercised and worked: - `supported`: the changed path ran, replaced the diagnosed waste, and the measured movement supports the mechanism. - `partially_supported`: it worked on only part of the path or one objective. - `unsupported`: the path did not run or did not replace the target behavior. - `contradicted`: the path ran but added work or caused the opposite behavior. - `unmeasured`: the current scenarios did not exercise the mechanism. Also record causal attribution as `patch_caused`, `stochastic`, `mixed`, or `uncertain`. Mechanism verdict and causal attribution are analysis outputs; objective movement, train screening, and MOO status are machine inputs. [...] - **`quality_gain_cost_loss`**: Did extra work causally buy the quality gain? If development-evaluated, did it produce nondominated admissible point? - **`cost_gain_quality_loss`**: Did savings come from removing waste or from skipping required work? Did the development admit it? [...] There are four independent classifications on every command: - `--status` is the exact-pass transition from the per-scenario table. - `--movement-label` is the machine-computed scenario movement. - `--mechanism-verdict` records whether the modified mechanism was exercised. - `--causal-attribution` records whether behavior was patch-caused, stochastic, mixed, or uncertain.

sections.title: L LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Evaluation cost and uncertainty. Repeated executions improve optimization evidence but increase evaluation cost. Our Bayesian bootstrap captures variation among executions on fixed screening tasks, rather than uncertainty from task sampling. Future work could jointly adapt task selection and repetition counts to allocate evaluation effort where promotion decisions remain uncertain. Beyond Pareto-aware promotion. Our promotion rule provides one operational definition of promising intermediate candidate. Other local gates could preserve candidates that improve particular task instances or exhibit novel behaviors, even without favorable aggregate qualitycost changes. An LLM-based gate could also use execution traces and optimization history to judge whether candidate warrants broader development evaluation. Evaluating these alternatives would clarify how to balance immediate gains, potential for later improvement, and screening cost.
